analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks while in office.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration, where it sat with no further action as of the end of the record.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal ethics law to bar sitting members of Congress and their spouses from buying, selling, or holding individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, or similar derivatives. It would allow only widely diversified mutual funds and ETFs, plus Treasury bonds, and would give current members 180 days to sell off holdings. Violators would have to return any profits to the Treasury and could face civil fines equal to 10 percent of the value of each non-compliant holding, escalating every 30 days, with enforcement by the House and Senate ethics committees and an audit by the Government Accountability Office.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens get a clearer rule: the people who vote on laws affecting companies could not personally bet on those companies' stocks — or have a spouse do it — while in office. Investors and citizens who believe lawmakers' votes should not line their own portfolios gain an enforceable standard, with fines and public compliance records. Members themselves would keep a path to invest through diversified funds and Treasury bonds.

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress and their spouses could no longer hold, buy, or sell individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, or look-alike derivatives like options while the member is in office.

Members who violate the ban must hand over to the Treasury any profit from a violating transaction and face civil fines of 10 percent of the value of each non-divested holding, charged every 30 days until they comply.
Members must certify compliance annually, the certifications and fines are published online, and the Government Accountability Office must audit compliance two years after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest individual stocks, options, commodities, and similar holdings within 180 days or face escalating fines and forced repayment of profits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Enforcement sits with the House and Senate ethics committees, which are made up of the members' own colleagues; a member can also appeal a fine to a floor vote of the whole chamber, so punishment ultimately depends on other members of Congress.
Members and spouses get 180 days after enactment to sell their holdings, and ethics committees may grant extensions for good-faith divestment efforts, so the ban would not take effect immediately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is to members of Congress who would have to sell or give up direct control of individual stocks, stock options, and commodities during their terms — real sacrifices for some, but arguably the price of holding office where votes move markets. The main cost to the public is none that the record identifies; the bill keeps the disclosure apparatus and ethics-committee enforcement it builds on, and congressional ethics committees' uneven record of policing their own members is a fair concern, which is why the mandatory fines and GAO audit matter. On balance the trade is public trust and cleaner incentives for a modest restriction on what elected officials and their spouses may invest in.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and sent to the House committee that handles congressional operations, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, no movement.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Alford introduced the bill on May 14, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day.
After the referral, no committee action, markup, or floor vote appears in the record.
The Congress remains in session through January 2027, so the bill can still move, but a bill that sits in committee without a hearing typically does not reach the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and their spouses, who keep their ability to trade individual stocks and commodities while in office.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who keep trading rights

for.name: Rep. Mark Alford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: House Committee on House Administration
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no recorded action on it since May 2025.

sides.party_line_note: With only one cosponsor and no votes or committee action on record, there is not enough information to tell how the bill splits by party.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The people who write laws affecting companies would be barred from holding or trading those companies' securities, or from having a spouse do so, with fines and profit disgorgement for violations.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors beyond one and has sat without action since May 2025. At this stage in a two-year Congress, bills with this level of committee inactivity rarely reach the floor unless leadership decides to prioritize them.
